verses.text: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the inland regions and reached Ephesus. There he found some disciples.
He asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said, “No—we haven’t even heard there is a Holy Spirit.”
“Then what baptism did you receive?” he asked. They said, “John’s baptism.”
Paul explained, “John baptized people as they turned back to God. He told them to believe in the one coming after him—that is, Jesus.”
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul placed his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them. They spoke in other languages and prophesied.
There were about twelve men altogether.
Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, discussing and persuading people about God’s Kingdom.

But some became stubborn and refused to believe. They spoke against the Way in front of everyone, so Paul left them and took the disciples with him. Every day he taught in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so that everyone living in Asia heard the Lord’s message about Jesus—Jews and Greeks alike.
God did extraordinary miracles through Paul.
When cloths or work aprons that had touched him were carried to the sick, their illnesses left and evil spirits came out.
Some traveling Jewish exorcists tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over people with evil spirits. They would say, “I command you by the Jesus Paul preaches.”
Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.
But the evil spirit answered, “I know Jesus, and I know Paul—but who are you?”
Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them. He beat them so badly they ran out of the house naked and wounded.
Everyone in Ephesus—Jews and Greeks alike—heard about this. Fear came over them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was honored.
Many who had become believers came forward, openly admitting and describing what they had done.
A number who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them in front of everyone. They calculated their value: fifty thousand silver coins.
In this way the Lord’s message spread and showed its power.
After all this, Paul decided in the Spirit to travel through Macedonia and Achaia and then go to Jerusalem. “After that,” he said, “I must also see Rome.”
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, ahead to Macedonia, while he stayed in Asia a little longer.
Around that time, a major disturbance broke out over the Way.
A silversmith named Demetrius made silver shrines of Artemis and brought plenty of business to the craftsmen.
He gathered them and other workers in the same trade and said, “Men, you know this work brings us good money.
“You can see and hear that not just here in Ephesus but throughout nearly all Asia, Paul has persuaded many people and turned them away. He says gods made by human hands aren’t really gods.

“So there’s a real danger our trade will lose respect. And the temple of the great goddess Artemis could be dismissed as nothing; her greatness could be brought down—even though all Asia and the world worship her!”
When they heard this, they became furious and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
Confusion swept through the whole city. The crowd rushed together into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s Macedonian traveling companions.
Paul wanted to go in and address the crowd, but the disciples wouldn’t let him.
Even some officials from Asia who were his friends sent him a message, begging him not to risk going into the theater.
Some people shouted one thing, others something else. The gathering was completely confused, and most people didn’t even know why they were there.
The crowd brought Alexander forward. The Jews had pushed him to the front, and he motioned with his hand, hoping to make a defense to the people.
But when the crowd realized he was Jewish, everyone shouted together, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” They kept it up for about two hours.
At last the city clerk quieted the crowd and said, “People of Ephesus, everyone knows our city is the guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and her image that fell from Zeus.
“Since no one can deny this, calm down. Don’t do anything reckless.
“You brought these men here, but they haven’t robbed temples or insulted our goddess.
“So if Demetrius and the craftsmen have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and there are proconsuls. They can bring charges there.
“If you have another matter, it can be settled in the regular assembly.
“We’re at risk of being charged with starting a riot today, and we have no good reason to give for this uproar.”
After he said this, he dismissed the assembly.
